sections.heading: Architecture Overview
content: This setup runs a fully autonomous multi-agent software development pipeline across two physical machines in a home lab. Three AI agents — Product Manager, Engineering Agent, and DevOps Agent — communicate asynchronously via a self-hosted Forgejo instance to triage issues, write code, review pull requests, run quality checks, deploy to staging, and ship production releases to the homelab’s bare-metal host.

The agents run as Linux users on a VM called Lion's Rest Inn, hosted on the Canterbury Unraid server. Each agent has its own Forgejo user identity, Hermes profile, OpenRouter API key, SSH key, and GPG signing key. They are fully independent and communicate only through Forgejo issues, PRs, and reviews — no SSH, no file handoffs, no direct API calls between agents.
Traffic flow: Stakeholder → Telegram or SSH CLI → PM Agent → Forgejo issues → Engineering Agent → Pull Requests → PM Review → DevOps Pipeline → Staging + Production Deploy → Stakeholder merges.

The git host is Forgejo (git.chrisharrsch.com) running as a Docker container on Canterbury with a PostgreSQL backend, fronted by Nginx Proxy Manager. The previous GitHub org was replaced by Forgejo after GitHub's machine-account ToS limits capped the number of agent identities on a free plan — self-hosting removes the limit entirely. The full Forgejo deployment process is documented in the Self-Hosted Git with Forgejo guide.

Stack: Three Hermes Agent v0.19.0 instances (uv tool install, no venvs), each with its own model and budget, running on Ubuntu 24.04 with Docker for staging deployments, plus an mTLS Docker context to the Canterbury bare-metal host for production. All LLM calls go through OpenRouter.

sections.heading: Agent Setup Pattern
sections.subtitle: Every agent follows this identical bootstrap procedure. Captured as a reusable skill in the agent-onboarding skill in the skill library.
steps: Create Linux user on the Agent VM with Docker group access
Generate SSH key and GPG signing key (ed25519)
Create Forgejo user account with plus-addressed email (harrsch.agents+<agent>@gmail.com)
Upload SSH public key + GPG public key, add to Harrsch-Industries org under the agents team
Generate a Forgejo PAT (scopes: write:repository, write:issue, read:user, read:admin)
Install Hermes via uv tool install hermes-agent --python python3 (never a local venv)
Write config.yaml with model, provider, and persona system prompt
Wire PAT via tea login add and register the git credential helper (tea login helper setup), deploy the forgejo-api wrapper script
Create cron jobs with --workdir /home/<agent> to avoid .git permission errors

sections.heading: PR Review Workflow
sections.subtitle: A three-tier review system that ties all agents together. Saved as a reusable skill in the skill library.
content: Work is event-driven through Forgejo's own organization webhook: it posts issue and pull-request events straight to the receiver on the staging VM, so agent triggers need no CI workflow and no polling. Pull requests fall into three tiers:
Tier 1 — Auto-Approve (auto-approve label): For dependency bumps, CI config changes, minor docs, pure refactors. PM sanity-checks then squash-merges automatically. No human involvement.

Tier 2 — PM Review + Ping (pm-review label, default): PM reviews the diff for hardcoded secrets, injection vectors, missing auth, debug code, missing tests, logic errors, and breaking API changes. If clean: approves (does not merge) and sends a Telegram notification to the stakeholder with a summary.
Tier 3 — Escalate (human-review label or critical findings): PM flags the stakeholder immediately on Telegram.

If PM finds issues in Tier 2, they submit a formal Forgejo review requesting changes. The Engineering Agent is triggered by the event pipeline, reads the review comments, fixes the code, pushes, and re-requests review from the PM.
After the PM approves, the DevOps Agent runs a 4-stage pipeline. If all stages pass, it also approves. The PR then sits with two approvals waiting for the stakeholder's final review and merge.

main is protected on every repository. Direct pushes are refused, one approval is required, stale approvals are dismissed when new commits land, and an outdated branch cannot be merged. Repository admins do not bypass this — only a site admin can.

An agent that tries to push to main gets 403 user cannot commit to repo. That is the guardrail working as intended. The recovery is a branch and a pull request: never a force-push, never a retry loop, and never a request to lift the protection. The rule is stated once, briefly, in the deploy skill rather than repeated in every prompt — the agents are meant to learn the mechanics by hitting them.

sections.heading: DevOps Pipeline Stages
content: The DevOps Agent runs this pipeline on every new or updated PR that passes PM review:
1. Code Quality — Linting (ruff for Python, ESLint for JS), type checking (mypy), security scan (bandit), secrets detection. All stage failures block the pipeline.
2. Build & Tests — Install dependencies, run unit tests (pytest, npm test), check coverage. All tests must pass.
3. Staging Deploy — Docker Compose build and deploy to /home/staging/, verify healthcheck endpoint, run integration tests. Stacks are isolated by project and PR number.
4. Cleanup & Report — Tear down the staging stack, post a PR comment with per-stage pass/fail results. If all pass: approve the PR. If any fail: request changes with details.

The Security Bot then performs a separate deep-dive audit on the final code and staging deployment — static analysis (OWASP Top 10, dependency CVEs, secret detection) plus dynamic checks on the running instance. Critical findings block the merge; lower-severity findings are filed as recommendations.

Forgejo Actions now handles deployment work only: the production-deploy workflow below is the one remaining workflow, because a deploy is not an event Forgejo can webhook. Agent triggers come from the org webhook.
Production deploys go to the Canterbury bare-metal host over a dedicated mTLS Docker context — see the section below.

sections.heading: Production Deploys (Canterbury)
content: Production releases run on the same bare-metal Unraid host that already runs Forgejo and Nginx Proxy Manager. The DevOps agent drives it through a dedicated Docker context over TLS — mutual TLS with a client certificate issued specifically for hi-devops-agent — so production access is authenticated and revoked by certificate, not by shared credentials.

When a PR labeled deploy:prod is merged to main, the repo’s .forgejo/workflows/production-deploy.yml fires, POSTs an X-Gitea-Event: production_deploy webhook to the local receiver (port 8899), and the receiver routes it to the DevOps agent. The agent loads the devops/production-deploy skill and follows it exactly:

1. Preflight — parse the PR’s Deploy: block (subdomain, port, healthcheck, websockets), verify the canterbury context, check the host port is free, confirm no NPM proxy conflict, and refuse with a deploy-failed label on any problem.

2. Environment — compare the repo’s .env.example variable names against the agent’s prod-env/<repo>.env (names only, never values). Missing file or keys → comment on the PR, label deploy-failed, stop.
3. Checkout & build — clone at the exact merge commit SHA, then docker --context canterbury compose build then up -d under the prod-<repo> project name.
4. Route — create or update the Nginx Proxy Manager host via its API (wildcard Let’s Encrypt certificate, force SSL, HTTP/2, websocket support per the Deploy block).
5. Verify — three health checks: direct to the container port, through NPM on the LAN, and the public URL, retried for up to 90 seconds.
6. Report — comment the result on the PR, set the deployed (or deploy-failed) label, and write deploy.json so future merges redeploy with the same settings.
First deploy through this pipeline: learning-roadmap → learn.chrisharrsch.com (2026-10-27), all three health checks green, label and report handled entirely by the agent.
Key lessons from productionizing this path:

• The webhook receiver’s prompt templates support exactly four variables ({number}, {title}, {url}, {repo}) — any other placeholder (e.g. {ref}) crashes the route with a KeyError and silently drops the deploy event.

• The TLS client key and the CA key that signs it live on Canterbury’s flash storage and must never be deleted — losing the CA key makes it impossible to issue new client certificates, which blocks the docker context entirely.

• With a remote context, bind-mount sources resolve on Canterbury, not on the agent VM. Persistent data belongs in named volumes or a persistent appdata path on Canterbury’s array, never in the checkout.
• Every production command names the canterbury context explicitly — a bare docker compose silently targets staging.
• The labels deploy:prod, deployed, and deploy-failed plus the PR’s Deploy: block are the pipeline’s handshake — the only deploy instructions the agent follows.

sections.heading: Agent Communication
content: All inter-agent communication happens through Forgejo. No agent ever SSHes into another or reads another agent's files. This eliminates coupling between agent runtimes and keeps a full audit trail on the Forgejo instance.
PM → Eng: Creates issues with requirements, assigns to the engineering agent's Forgejo user. Action triggers the event pipeline immediately.
Eng → PM: Opens PRs with labels. Comments on issues with status updates. Re-requests review after addressing feedback.
PM → Stakeholder: Telegram notifications for PRs ready for review, escalations, and status summaries.
DevOps → PRs: Pipeline reports as PR comments. Approves or requests changes based on pipeline outcome.
Delay between any action and downstream processing is near-instant — the Forgejo Act Runner picks up new jobs within seconds and fires the agent.

sections.heading: Skills & Knowledge Base
content: All reusable agent workflows are saved as Hermes skills (markdown files with YAML frontmatter that agents can load as procedural memory):

agent-onboarding — Full bootstrap procedure: Linux user, SSH/GPG keys, Hermes install, config, git setup, Forgejo PAT wiring, cron creation. Includes email convention, PATH pitfalls, and gateway setup.
pr-review-workflow — Three-tier PR approval system. Covers the decision matrix, tea CLI commands for each tier, and the agent feedback loop.

production-deploy — The full Canterbury deploy procedure: preflight rules, Deploy: block parsing, env-file comparison, build/up over the remote context, NPM proxy host management, three-stage health verification, rollback rules, and the report/label protocol.
Both skills live at Harrsch-Industries/skill-library under devops/<skill>/SKILL.md.
A master configuration reference (AGENTS.md) tracks every agent's specific SSH key fingerprint, GPG key ID, model, budget, cron job ID, and Forgejo PAT for maintenance.

sections.heading: Cost Notes
content: All agents use OpenRouter with independent daily budget caps. No keys are shared.

The PM and DevOps agents use a cost-effective model since most of their work is executing terminal commands (git, tea, docker) rather than heavy reasoning. The Engineering Agent gets a stronger, more expensive model and the largest budget since it does the actual coding.
Agents are event-triggered via a Forgejo organization webhook (issue and pull-request events) plus one Actions workflow for deploys

sections.heading: Changelog
content: 2026-10-30v4Webhook reality check and PR-only mainReplaced the per-repo agent-trigger.yml workflows with a single organization-level Forgejo webhook, and found three ways that setup fails silently: an event selection saved with nothing ticked, Forgejo's SSRF protection refusing a private receiver address until it is allowlisted in app.ini, and a receiver keyed to the Gitea event header when Forgejo sends X-Forgejo-Event. Delivery now proves itself: a PR opening fires the PM agent with no hand-posted events. Then closed the other half of the loop — main is branch-protected on every repo (no direct pushes, one approval, stale approvals dismissed, outdated branches blocked), so agent changes land as pull requests or not at all. Also swept four empty NPM access lists left behind by the deploy agent: an access list with zero clients allows everything while looking like a gate. That guard, and the rule that scratch lists are deleted in the run that creates them, went into the production-deploy skill.

2026-10-27v3Production deploys to CanterburyThe DevOps agent now ships merged apps to the bare-metal host through the event pipeline. First production deploy: learning-roadmap → learn.chrisharrsch.com (health checks 200 direct/LAN/public, deployed label set by the agent). Root cause of the first missed deploy: the webhook receiver had no route for the production_deploy event when the PR was merged (logged “No route — ignored”), and the route added afterwards used an unsupported {ref} template variable, crashing on every replay. Fixed the receiver route, installed the devops/production-deploy skill, and provisioned the mTLS canterbury Docker context with a dedicated hi-devops-agent client certificate.

2026-10-10v2Event-driven pipelineReplaced all polling crons with Forgejo Actions + Act Runner. The eng-agent’s pr-issue-poller had run 6,516 times in ~9 weeks before being replaced. Deployed a Forgejo Act Runner (lions-rest-inn-vm) on the staging VM, added .forgejo/workflows/agent-trigger.yml to all repos, and a webhook receiver (systemd, port 8899) routing events to the correct agent. All agent crons paused. Verified end-to-end.
